doc.title: Derrick Gardner interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 9, 2013

title: Composing from a Foster voicing and Randy Gillespie's drum beat
summary: Ideas can come from anywhere; one tune came from a saxophone voicing Foster showed him, another from a beat by drummer Randy Gillespie.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: I want to see if this will work for me. I want to ask you about something here.
I think I’ve kind of heard this before.
So where does the idea come from for a song like that.

It can come from anywhere. It can come from any and all directions. Sometimes you hear the melody first, sometimes you hear a chord progression first, sometimes you hear a rhythmic beat that might influence it. I’ve written pieces from all directions. That particular piece came from a voicing that Frank Foster showed me on the piano for a big © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -7-

band, or a saxophone section voicing, that’s very spread out. As a matter of fact it’s fifths between the baritone, second tenor, and then fifths between the first tenor, second alto and lead alto. And then you fit the trombones in between the spaces there. It’s a real big, thick sounding chord. And so he was showing me this voicing for the saxophones and I was checking it out and I said man, that’s nice. And then I kind of started moving things around here and said wait a minute, what’s this? And I said oh, oh, I like this. So I wrote a tune based off of that voicing, added a melody to it you know. And there was another tune that I wrote from a particular rhythmic beat or feel, that a wonderful friend of mine that I used to teach with at the Michigan State University, his name is Randy Gillespie, one of the unsung legends on drums. I mean this guy sounds like Roy Haynes or Art Blakey or any of them, or Elvin Jones. He used to be the drummer with Sonny Stitt and Wes Montgomery back in the day. And he was teaching drums at Michigan State. And we were on this gig one time and he started playing this particular beat that was just as significant as say you know the beat on Ahmad Jamal’s “Poinciana?” You know? Something as significant. It’s different but it’s as significant as that. And he broke it out. We were trading, and I did my four bars trading, and he broke out this beat. And I said man what is that? And he just smiled at me you know, and said “yeah, I got you here.” So after the gig I said “man, do that thing you were doing when we were trading fours.” And so he explained to me that when he was playing with — the organist, I can’t think of the organist’s name — they were playing Atlantic City. And they were opening for Jimmy Smith. Gene Lovey. He was playing with Gene Lovey. And they were opening for Jimmy Smith. And they were covering a Ray Charles tune or something. And he said he broke out this beat, and he said all of a sudden the crowd got up and started dancing and everything and getting all hyped and everything. And then he played that thing for an hour. I said wow man. And then after he finished Jimmy Smith came over to him and said “I don’t know why they got us coming on, y’all done burned up the stage, man. We can’t play after that.”
